7.0.s.en: 1. His days are like the days of a hireling, full of misery

7.0.0.en: 1 Is there not a struggle for man upon earth? and are not his days also like the days of an hireling? 2 As a servant earnestly desireth the shadow, and as an hireling looketh for the reward of his work: 3 So am I made to possess months of vanity, and wearisome nights are appointed to me. 4 When I lie down, I say, When shall I arise? the night is long, and I am full of tossings to and fro unto the dawning of the day. 5 My flesh is clothed with worms and clods of dust; my skin is broken, and become loathsome. 6 My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle, and are spent without hope.

7.0.1.en: Is not the life of man a struggle upon earth, and are not his days also like the days of an hireling? [1]

7.0.2.en: Job seeks an excuse for himself even in the extremity of his longing for death, supporting his opinion with the fact that the whole of man's life is toil, for he is "of few days, and full of trouble" (Job 14:1). Every man realizes that his days are few, and has justification for longing for death soon; therefore he wonders how they could regard him as having committed a heinous crime when he longed for it.

7.0.3.en: By saying "upon earth," which God has given to the children of men (Ps 115:16), he points to the lowliness of man, for his dwelling place is still below on earth, and not among the heavenly orders. Truly, he does not dwell in hell as the enemy of the good does, but for a time on earth. We live here temporarily, governed not by the fate of the Stoics nor the blind chance of the Epicureans, but by the counsel of God and His high, heavenly, divine plan.

7.0.4.en: As for the state of man here, it is "a struggle... like the days of an hireling," a state of continual striving, like soldiers in a battle that does not stop. Our enemies do not cease to oppose us, and they do not sleep at night. By death the battle is decided, either that we may be crowned eternally or be in shame and disgrace.

7.0.5.en: Our days are like the days of a hireling: we work all day long to give account at its end. Like a hireling who wishes the day to end quickly so that he may rest from the exhaustion of continual work. The hireling welcomes the passing of the day and the coming of night for rest, as the watchman rejoices at the passing of the night with the light of morning (Ps 130:6). The hireling longs for the end of the day, because "the sleep of a labouring man is sweet" (Eccl 5:12).

7.0.6.en: * Is not the life of man upon earth a struggle, and his life like the days of an hireling? Like the servant who lurks in the shadow for fear of his master, or like the hireling who looks for his wages? So also I wait for empty months and wearisome nights appointed to me. If I lie down I say, When will the day dawn? And if I arise I say again, When will evening come? I am full of pain from night until the dawn of morning. My body is putrid with the corruption of worms, and I have wetted the clods of the earth by scratching my sores, which discharge pus! My days are more trifling than empty talk, and are spent without hope. I say: [My bed will comfort me], but You [scare me with dreams, and terrify me through visions] (Job 1:7-6, 13-14) LXX.

7.0.7.en: * How wretched is the state of man! Like a hireling, he toils and labors for others while he himself is in want! And he cannot support himself except through the sympathy of others! Every day he endures a bitter bondage under the oppression of fear and dread. And lest his master seize him, he thinks he can hide from him in the shadow of this world, the wandering, roving, fleeing shadow! Think of the one of whom Sirach speaks in the book of the Wisdom of Sirach, Ecclesiasticus: [Every man sins on his bed, despising and saying to himself, Who sees me? Darkness is around me, and the walls hide me; whom do I fear?] (Sir 23:25-26). Do not think that such a man is a prodigal hireling...? Like the young man in the Gospel, of whom we read that he received his portion of the inheritance from his father, and when he came to be in want and in need, began to feed the flocks of others as a means of satisfying his hunger and paying his expenses with what he received (Lk 11:15-16); but he at least finally came to himself and repented, for he returned to his father, and did not conceal his sins but disclosed them.

7.0.8.en: But the man who thinks that God does not see him, He who sees everything, and that his iniquities can be hidden by darkness, lives in the shadow; yet he vainly thinks that he escapes observation, for the eye of the Lord, brighter than the sun, uncovers all secrets and hidden things, lights up every darkness, enters into the knowledge of the depth of the heart, and penetrates the heights and the depths (Jn 19:3-20; Sir 23:28). Therefore the man who thinks he is under the protection of darkness thinks in vain; for he cannot escape from the light that shines in the darkness, and the darkness comprehended it not (Jn 5:1).

7.0.9.en: Hence he is discovered as a fugitive and a wicked hireling, and is recognized before he can hide himself! For all things are known to the Lord before He examines them, not only with regard to past events, but future ones also.

7.0.10.en: * Whoever thinks that he hides his crime is lost in an empty hope, for that is mere feeble talk and not the truth. Truly, [the talk of sinners is empty and hateful] (Sir 27:14); it yields no fruit, only weeping! For [the talk of a fool is like a burden in the way] (Sir 21:19), and what is sin but a weight? It is a weight on the shoulders of the wayfarer in this world, so that he is weighed down with a heavy load of guilt! If he is unwilling to submit to the carrying of the burden, he must turn to the Lord who said: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Mt 28:11).

7.0.11.en: St. Ambrose * God is in His saints when they are tried, and holiness follows trial. It is impossible for anyone, even a saint, to pass through this world without trial. As Job says: [The life of man upon earth is a struggle (warfare)] (Job 7:1).

7.0.12.en: * We read in the book of Job how, while the first messenger of evil was yet speaking, there came also another (Job 1:16). And in the same book it is written: [Is there not here a trial?](a) and according to the better Hebrew text: "There is a warfare against man upon earth." We strive in this life that we may be crowned in the life to come, and for this purpose we risk our lives in the battle of this world (Mt 4:1-11)(b). Scripture testifies of Abraham that God tried him (Gen 22:1-19). For this reason also the Apostle says: [We glory in tribulations... knowing that tribulation worketh patience, and patience hope, and now hope maketh not ashamed] (cf. Rom 5:3-5). And in another place: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? As it is written, For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter" (Rom 8:35-36). The prophet Isaiah comforts such persons with the words: [You who are weaned from the milk, drawn from the breasts, behold trial upon trial, yea, and hope upon hope] (Isa 28:9-10) LXX. As the Apostle expressed it: "The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us" (Rom 8:18).

7.0.13.en: St. Jerome * When you flee from Egypt you come to very high ascents of work and faith. You face a tower, a sea and waves. The way of life is not traveled without the waves of trials. The Apostle says: "All that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution" (2 Tim 3:12). Job also declared no less than this: [Our life upon earth is a trial] (Job 7:1).

7.0.14.en: Origen * Job in turn repeated the saying of Eliphaz: Yet man is born unto trouble (Job 5:7). What does this mean for Job? He came to the final conclusion that this is not the only injustice, but that it springs from the very nature of man, which provokes these trials, as God decrees that the life of man must be painful. But Job added "upon earth," since it will no longer be so "in heaven."

7.0.15.en: St. John Chrysostom * What is this life but a fullness of snares?

7.0.16.en: We walk among snares (Sir 9:20); we live among many trials. [What is the life of man upon earth but a state of trial?] (Job 7:1) LXX.

7.0.17.en: He did well to add "upon earth," because there is one whose life is in heaven.

7.0.18.en: His life "upon earth" is the wages of a hireling, all toil and distress, feebler than vain tales (Job 7:1-2, 6) LXX, swimming in words and overflowing with words.

7.0.19.en: Its dwelling is in houses of clay, and life itself is mire. There is no steadiness of mind, nor endurance. By day man longs for night, and by night he seeks the day (cf. Job 7:4).

7.0.20.en: St. Ambrose * The evils that come upon you will pass, and he whom you await with patience will come. He will wipe away the sweat of toil. He will dry every tear, and there will be no more weeping. Here below we must groan amid trials, as Job asks: "[What is the life of man upon earth but a trial?"] (Job 7:1).

7.0.21.en: * My evil sorrows contend with my good joys, and on which side victory will be won I do not know.

7.0.22.en: Woe is me! Have mercy on me, O Lord!

7.0.23.en: Woe is me! Behold, I have not hidden my wounds!

7.0.24.en: You are the Physician, and I am sick.

7.0.25.en: You are merciful and I am wretched. [Is not the life of man upon earth a trial?]

7.0.26.en: Who desires sources of provocation and hardships? You command that we endure troubles, not that we love them.

7.0.27.en: You have commanded us to endure, not to love them. For there is no man who loves what he endures, though he must endure.

7.0.28.en: * Do not think that you are without sin while you are in this life, for we read of this in Holy Scripture: [Is not the life of man upon earth a trial?] Therefore, as long as we are in this body, you must say in prayer, as the Lord taught us: [Forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive them that trespass against us]. Remember to forgive quickly. If anyone sins against you and asks forgiveness, then you can pray sincerely and obtain forgiveness of your sins.

7.0.29.en: * [Human life upon earth is a trial] (Job 1:7) LXX; no one is ever in complete safety, nor ought he to be, until he comes to that city from which no friend departs and into which no enemy enters. Now, while we are in the very glory of the Church, we recognize the voices of our trials, and as members of Christ we submit to our Head in the bond of love, and support one another with a common spirit, and we say from the Psalms what we find in them about the martyrs who went before us, saying that trials are common to all men from the beginning to the end.

7.0.30.en: * The more (a person) loves his heavenly homeland, the more his earthly journey becomes in itself a great trial... In this trial, that is, in this life, whoever stands firm above it seeks God.

7.0.31.en: * You women indeed live in chastity, holiness, purity and virginity, and yet what is your life here? Are you not humbled when you hear: [What is human life upon earth but a trial?] (Job 7:1) LXX?

7.0.32.en: Does not the saying: [Woe unto the world because of offences!] (Mt 18:7) draw you away from self-reliance in pride?

7.0.33.en: Are you not afraid lest you be counted among the many whose love waxes cold because iniquity abounds (Mt 24:12)?

7.0.34.en: Do you not beat your breasts when you hear: "Let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall" (1 Cor 10:12)?

7.0.35.en: Amid these divine warnings and human dangers, do we find it hard to urge holy virgins to humility?

7.0.36.en: * It is not fitting for any man to feel secure in this life, which in its entirety is called a trial (Job 1:7). For he who has been able to attain a better state than the evil he was in, let him not turn from the better to the worse. Our only hope, our only confidence and our only sure promise is Your mercies.

7.0.37.en: * I say: Oh! that I had wings like a dove! for then would I fly away, and be at rest!

7.0.38.en: Then I would wander far off and remain in the wilderness.

7.0.39.en: Yet even in the wilderness I shall perhaps have the same experience, for it is said: [I waited for him that saveth me from faintness and from the tempest] (Ps 55:8) LXX.

7.0.40.en: Truly, the life of man upon earth is a life of trial.

7.0.41.en: * No one is certain of that eternal life which God, who cannot lie, promises to the children of the promise before the times of eternity. No one is certain unless he completes his life, which is a state of trial upon earth (Job 7:1). For God urges us to persevere in it until the end of this life, as we say to Him every day: "Lead us not into temptation" (Mt 6:13).

7.0.42.en: * There is no man of whom men can say with complete assurance that he is righteous until he departs from this world. For in his life, which is a trial upon earth, he that standeth must take heed lest he fall (1 Cor 10:12).

7.0.43.en: * There we shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is (1 Jn 3:1). But now, as long as the corruptible body presseth down the soul (Wis 9:15), and human life upon earth is wholly a trial (Job 7:1), in His sight shall no man living be justified (Ps 143:2).

7.0.44.en: * It has been shown sufficiently that in this life, which is wholly a trial, no one ought to boast as though he were free from all sins.

7.0.45.en: * Who but the proud man thinks he can live thus without needing to say to God: [Forgive us our debts]? Such a person is not a great man, but one puffed up with vanity, and an opponent of God, who giveth grace abundantly to the humble (Jas 4:6; 1 Pet 5:5).

7.0.46.en: St. Augustine * [Are not his days like the days of an hireling?]... So the days of man, when they are imbued with the knowledge of the truth and of eternal things, are compared to the days of a hireling, for he counts the present life as his road and not his city, a struggle and not the palms of victory. Seeing that he is far from his reward, he withdraws the more slowly to draw near to his goal...

7.0.47.en: Now it has been said by the voice of the Savior: "My kingdom is not of this world" (Jn 18:36). So all of us who have been given hope in heaven put on the troubles of the present life and busy ourselves with caring for others. For it often happens that even if we are compelled to serve the children of perdition, we oblige ourselves to render to the world what is the world's, and to care for what belongs to others, that we may receive the reward that is ours. So we busy ourselves faithfully with the affairs of others until we reach our reward. In contrast to this, the Truth says to some: [And if ye have not been faithful in that which is another man's, who shall give you that which is your own?] (Lk 16:12).

7.0.48.en: So the citizens of the upper land(c) say to their Creator the words of the Psalmist: [For thy sake we are killed all the day long] (Ps 44:22). And Paul says: [I die daily, brethren, for your glory] (cf. 1 Cor 15:31); and also: [For the which cause I also suffer these things: nevertheless I am not ashamed: for I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day] (2 Tim 1:12)...

7.0.49.en: * We should notice that he did not say that trial attends the life of man, but described it as having itself become a trial. For since (man) had freedom of will, he turned aside from the upright form in which he was created and became subject to a base state of corruption. While the life of man brought forth harm to itself from itself, it became itself the very thing into which it had fallen... The life of man has in a certain way become a "trial." For even if we restrain ourselves so as not to sin, while we practice good works the remembrance of evil works overshadows us with a mist of the soul.

7.0.51.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) presents to us many examples of how the life of man, even in his spiritual striving, has become a "trial" from which he suffers.

7.0.52.en: For example, he mentions that when a man strives to abstain from a luxurious life carried to excess, this abstinence or asceticism can become a trial for him. By asceticism his face becomes pale, and when others notice his pale face they consider him worthy of honor and praise him, and through their praise vainglory creeps into the mind of the ascetic.

7.0.53.en: He gives us another example: a man may be granted knowledge of the divine Law, and he rejoices that he has received more understanding than others, and is lifted up with a joy that carries selfishness, and by his haughtiness spoils the gift of understanding he has received. On the day of judgment his state will be worse than that of others by the very thing in which he appeared more splendid than others in this life.

7.0.54.en: Thus he presents many examples of various virtues that turn to his destruction because of the corruption of his nature, so that what is for edification becomes the very cause of his perdition, because his life is a "trial."

7.0.55.en: St. Augustine asks, since it is said in the book of Job [Is not the life of man upon earth a trial?] (Job 1:7) LXX, why do we pray: "Lead us not into temptation"?

7.0.56.en: He answers that we must distinguish between two kinds of trials. The first kind is that in which there is an inducement to sin; of this it is said: "Let no man say when he is tempted, I am tempted of God" (Jas 13:1). And there is a trial for proving, of which it is said: "For the Lord your God proveth (trieth) you, to know whether ye love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul" (Deut 3:13). God knows what is in the heart; what is meant here is "that we ourselves know" what is in our hearts.

7.0.57.en: * This I know, that the life of man upon earth is a trial (Job 1:7), and that there is a heavy yoke upon the sons of Adam (Sir 1:40). But what pleases me the more is to discuss the question concerning this building, when we say that we are sojourners or strangers on earth, since we have found our upper city, where we receive the earnest here, and when we reach it we shall not leave it.

7.1.0.en: St. Augustine As a servant earnestly desireth the shadow, and as an hireling looketh for the reward of his work [2].

7.1.1.en: The servant who toils in the heat of the day longs for the shadow; so Job longs to depart from the day of this world by death, to find shade in the grave.

7.1.2.en: The lengthening of the shadow points to the end of the day with its toils, when the worker longs to end his day. In India time was measured by the length of a person's shadow. When a man was asked about the length of his working day, he was asked to stand in a sunny place and the length of his shadow was measured, and they would tell him the time. So the one who wishes to leave his work often says, How long is my coming shadow?

7.1.3.en: * "Deliver me, O Lord, from mine enemies: I flee unto thee to hide me" (Ps 9:143). I who once fled from You, now flee to You. Adam fled from the face of God and hid among the trees of paradise, and of him it is said in the book of Job: [As a servant fleeing from his master, and finds a shadow] (Job 2:7) LXX. He fled from the face of his master and found a shadow. Woe to him if he continues in the shadow, lest it be said afterward: [All those things are passed away like a shadow] (Wis 5:9).

7.1.4.en: St. Augustine * [Like a servant who eagerly longs for the shadow, and a hireling who looks for the end of his work, so I possess months of vanity, and number wearisome nights...](d) Paul runs panting to lay hold of this shadow, longing to depart and to be with Christ (Phil 1:23). This shadow is already possessed by those who say with all the desire of their hearts: "We have borne the burden and heat of the day" (Mt 20:12)... This is the reason why Paul is always lifted up with boldness in the face of calamities, for he is [like a hireling who looks for the end of his work]... for he declares that he was burdened above strength, saying: "We were pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life" (2 Cor 1:8). But how he wiped away from his soul the streams of this great toil with the towel of his reward, he tells us himself, saying: "For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us" (Rom 8:18). Thus, as a hireling looking for the end of his work, he is concerned to increase the reward.

7.2.0.en: So am I made to possess months of vanity, and wearisome nights are appointed to me [3].

7.2.1.en: In the midst of his suffering Job reckoned that his whole life had been wasted without profit, and thought that all the months of his life were evil and his nights misery. After the trial he was unable in his sickness to work, so he forgot all that he had done before in the days of his health and prosperity, but God will not forget them. He felt that his presence on earth was a burden on the community, for he was without work, and he did not realize how the Creator of heaven and earth cherishes him, and how many are blessed through him.

7.2.2.en: The believer longs for eternal rest as a shadow in which to take refuge after suffering the heat of the sun of trials and afflictions in this world. In this he realizes that his life is a short journey, not reaching a year or years, but counted months, vain months and cruel nights, nights of hardship and toil. It is a passing life, but toward a glorious eternity. The more we realize the shortness of time, the more we pass over rejoicing into eternity, indifferent to the heaviness of life and its troubles.

7.2.3.en: He counts our life as months of evil or months of vanity, and nights of evil or of hardship and toil, and they are counted and fixed, "appointed to us." He mentions the months that comprise the days, and does not forget the nights, for the believer cares about his salvation as a whole, or his life as one unit, as he cares about each night by itself. He cares about every small and great thing in his conduct, as about life as a whole.

7.2.4.en: When I lie down, I say, When shall I arise?

7.3.0.en: The night is long, and I am full of tossings to and fro unto the dawning of the day [4].

7.3.1.en: His nights became exceedingly long, because sleep found no place in him, so that the minutes hardly pass, and at the same time he does not look forward to a day in which he may find rest.

7.3.2.en: Neither place nor time gives true rest to man, but the inner peace of the heart; whoever flees from pains by sleeping at night finds in his sleep anxiety and terrors perhaps more severe than what he suffers by day.

7.3.3.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees in these words the cries of the holy Church as long as she is in this life full of corruption; she laments, unsatisfied with the instability in which she is. She wishes to ascend by constant contemplation of God in order to find rest in Him, and to fortify herself in Him so as to serve her Creator with love, so that corruption cannot approach her and touch her. Sin corrupted the life of man and deprived him of stability, so that he is in constant struggle: if he rests, as at night, he seeks to work, and if he works, he seeks to rest. Since sin made him lose the possession of God, his mind no longer finds rest. His true rest is in God, the fountain of rest.

7.3.4.en: Pope Gregory has another interpretation, which is that sleep here indicates falling into sin, which brings corruption on man.

7.3.5.en: * This also can be understood in another sense. For sleep is lying prostrate in sin. If sleep were not a symbol of sin, Paul could not have said to his disciples: "Awake to righteousness, and sin not" (1 Cor 15:34). For the same reason he entrusts to his hearer the following: "Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light" (Eph 5:14). And also: "It is high time to awake out of sleep" (Rom 13:11).

7.3.6.en: By consenting to evil practices we perish by corruption, and by allowing images of evil deeds to arise in the heart we are defiled with the stains of dust; therefore he says: "My flesh is clothed with the filth of dust."

7.3.8.en: My flesh is clothed with worms and clods of dust (clay).

7.4.0.en: My skin is broken, and become loathsome (my skin is cracked and festered) [5].

7.4.1.en: His sores bred worms that filled his body, so that the worms around his body in his wounds were like a garment he wore, and he could not be rid of them. The scabs of the sores became like heaps of dust, and his skin shrank and was torn. Thus who can describe the sight of Job, who had become like a heap of dust loaded with worms, with an exceedingly foul smell, corruption creeping in it; whoever looks at him is utterly disgusted.

7.4.2.en: * The sores of his body were preparing for him the crown of heaven.

7.5.0.en: St. Jerome My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle, and are spent without hope [6].

7.5.1.en: If Job longs for the swiftness of death, it is because his condition reveals it. He believed that his state was hastening him to the end of his life on earth, that only a few days were left to him, for naturally his body cannot resist this disease. His life ends without hope of returning to his former prosperity.

7.6.s.en: 2. Death puts an end to present misery

7.6.0.en: 7 O remember that my life is wind: mine eye shall no more see good. 8 The eye of him that hath seen me shall see me no more: thine eyes are upon me, and I am not. 9 As the cloud is consumed and vanisheth away: so he that goeth down to the grave shall come up no more. 10 He shall return no more to his house, neither shall his place know him any more.

7.6.1.en: O remember that my life is wind: mine eye shall no more see good [7].

7.6.2.en: Perhaps Job noticed that his friends, though they had not interrupted him in his speech, could no longer bear to look at him in his hideous appearance, nor to hear his voice; therefore he turned from speaking with them to speaking with God, for He alone is long-suffering, listens to wounded hearts, and does not scorn sick bodies however disfigured their appearance. He cried out to God, saying: "Remember that my life is wind." Thus Job wished to draw God's tenderness and compassion, as an exceedingly weak creature whose life passes swiftly without stopping, as the wind passes. As the Psalmist says: "Remember that they were but flesh; a wind that passeth away, and cometh not again" (Ps 78:38-39).

7.6.3.en: Thus Job kept before his eyes a plain truth about the shortness of life, and his certainty of his death and of not escaping it. This truth makes us not put our hope in the world, nor attach ourselves to visible things, nor be ruled by the things of the senses. For our happiness here consists in our realizing that we are strangers who must walk faithfully, and with a rejoicing spirit, until we pass over to our permanent dwelling.

7.6.4.en: * The eye of the dead sees good no more, for the soul no longer practices good works once it is stripped of the body. For this reason the rich man who was perishing in the fire of hell knew that he could not amend his state by good works, for he does not return again to practice what is for his good, but asked for his brothers whom he left behind: [I pray thee therefore, father Abraham, that thou wouldest send him to my father's house: for I have five brethren; that he may testify unto them, lest they also come into this place of torment] (Lk 16:27-28).

7.6.6.en: The eye of him that hath seen me shall see me no more.

7.7.0.en: Thine eyes are upon me, and I am not! [8]

7.7.1.en: Job noticed that his friends had surrounded him and sat around him seven days without speaking, but while looking at him they were like the blind, not seeing Job as he truly was; but the eyes of God look upon him in the midst of his trial, even though, because of the severity of the calamities, he appeared as one who does not exist, or who has lost his life and being!

7.7.2.en: Man needs the Lord's looking upon him, for He alone looks at the heart and is able to comfort him, and even to renew him. When our Lord Jesus, in the midst of His trial, looked at Simon Peter, he could not bear the eyes of the Master, and he went out and wept bitterly, until he met Him again after His resurrection, and He raised him from the tomb of his denial and restored him to his pastoral work!

7.7.3.en: Job in his trial realized that there is no way to complain about what had befallen him by God's permission except to lift his complaint to God Himself.

7.7.4.en: Time will pass quickly and those who now look at us will not see us; [we go hence, and are no more] (Ps 39:13); we leave what is visible to enjoy the invisible.

7.7.5.en: By saying "thine eyes are upon me, and I am not," the righteous Job reveals that he trusts in God's care and providence for him, and that He will send him to eternity to enjoy it, not by any merit on Job's part. Therefore he says: "I am not"; for my part I die, but who raises me up but You? And who brings me into glory but You?

7.7.6.en: * [The eye of man shall not see me] [8]. For the [eye of man] is the tenderness of the Savior, who softens the hardness of our dryness when He looks upon us. So the Gospel testifies, saying: "And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter. And Peter remembered the word of the Lord... And Peter went out, and wept bitterly" (Lk 22:61-62). But when the soul is stripped of the body, the "eye of man" no longer turns, for it will not save a man after his death, if grace did not grant him forgiveness before his death. Therefore Paul says: "Behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation" (2 Cor 6:2). So the Psalmist says: [For his mercy is for the one who is present] (cf. Ps 118:1).

7.7.7.en: Whoever is not rescued by mercy now, in the present state, is handed over by justice alone to punishment. Solomon says: "And if the tree fall toward the south, or toward the north, in the place where the tree falleth, there it shall be" (Eccl 11:3). For at the moment of the fall of the human being, the Holy Spirit or the evil spirit receives the soul departing from the chambers of the body, and that spirit keeps it forever without change.

7.7.8.en: If it has been glorified, it is not cast into woes; nor, if it is cast into eternal woes, does it rise again to find a means of escape...

7.7.9.en: After the present life, man no longer "sees with the eye of man," therefore he adds at once: [Thine eyes are upon me, and I am not standing!] as though saying in plain words: When You come in sternness to judgment You do not look in order to save, but look in order to punish. The person to whom You have not turned in the present time with Your saving, compassionate care, You look upon afterward by the law of justice.

7.7.11.en: As the cloud is consumed and vanisheth away.

7.8.0.en: So he that goeth down to the grave shall come up no more [9].

7.8.1.en: In his speech with God, Job confesses that he is going to his last abode without return to this world; his life here on earth is like a cloud that moves and vanishes without return.

7.8.2.en: * When it is said: [The dead praise not thee, O Lord] (Ps 115:17), this shows that this life alone is the appointed time for repentance and forgiveness. [And he that goeth down to hell shall come up no more] [9]; those who take pleasure in this life are the ones who will praise God. But those who died in sins have no time left to praise after death like those who enjoy blessings. Rather they lament over themselves, for praise belongs to him who gives thanks, and wailing to him who is under punishment. Therefore the godly rise to praise, but those who died in sins have no time for confession (thanksgiving) afterward.

7.8.3.en: * Concerning the phrase: [So he that goeth down to the grave shall come up no more] (Job 7:9). Notice what follows, "He shall return no more to his house"; and since the whole world will come to an end, and every house will be laid waste, how shall he return again to his house when there shall be a new earth, different? But they ought to have heard Job say: "For there is hope of a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again, and that the tender branch thereof will not cease. Though the root thereof wax old in the earth, and the stock thereof die in the ground; yet through the scent of water it will bud, and bring forth boughs like a plant. But man dieth, and wasteth away: yea, man giveth up the ghost, and where is he?"(e) He speaks with reproach and blame! He says, if the tree falls and lives again, shall not man live again, for whose sake all the trees exist? And lest you suppose that he sealed up the words, read what follows: and he says "If a man die, shall he live again?" (Job 14:14), and immediately adds: [I will wait till I rise]. And in another place: "And though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet without my flesh shall I see God" (Job 26:19). And in Isaiah: "Thy dead men shall live, together with my dead body shall they arise" (Isa 26:19). And in Ezekiel: "Behold, O my people, I will open your graves, and cause you to come up out of your graves" (Ezek 37:12). And in Daniel: "And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt" (Dan 2:12).

7.8.4.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem * It is as though he says plainly that whoever flies up on high (like the cloud) vanishes, for he boasts in himself, rushing to ruin.

7.8.5.en: * Rightly are the hearts of the despairing likened to clouds, for they become dark with the mist of error and dense with many sins, but when they vanish they pass away, for the flame of the last judgment shines upon them and they are scattered by the winds.

7.9.0.en: He shall return no more to his house, neither shall his place know him any more [10].

7.9.1.en: Job knows perfectly well that by his death he will no more return to his house in this world; he will own nothing, nor enjoy earthly things, nor carry on his temporal works. He leaves everything to the one who comes after him and takes his place.

7.9.2.en: "Neither shall his place know him any more": not only will Job not return to his place after his death, but the place and those who dwell in it will not know where Job is, for the connection between Job and those who live in his place is completely severed.

7.9.3.en: * Once a man is handed over to eternal punishments he is not called back again from there, where he could bind himself with love...

7.9.5.en: When the Lord Christ healed the demoniac, "he said unto him, Go home" (Mk 5:19), that is, return to his inner depths, taking care not to sin again; but after death a man cannot return to his house to amend his inner depths so as not to sin.

7.9.6.en: * Man was created to contemplate his Creator, so that he may always seek to be in His likeness, and dwell in the delight of His love. But if he is driven out of himself by disobedience, he loses the foundation of his mind. He is left outside in the dark ways, wandering far from the dwelling of the true light.

7.9.7.en: * "Neither shall his place know him any more": for the place of man, not a local place, has become the Creator Himself, who created him to be in Him, as a place for man. But he left the place when he listened to the words of the deceiver, forsaking the love of the Creator... Yet there are very many who, after receiving the help of the Savior, have sunk into the darkness of despair and perished again in extreme despair, as they despise the medicines of mercy offered to them. And rightly is it said of him who is condemned to eternal perdition: "Neither shall his place know him any more." It is to be noticed in particular that he does not say, "and he knows his place no more," but, "neither shall his place know him any more." For the word "know" is ascribed not to the person but to the place, which with firmness says in the end to those who dwell in evil: "I know you not whence ye are" (Lk 13:25).

7.10.s.en: 3. A description of his wretched state

7.10.0.en: 11 Therefore I will not refrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul. 12 Am I a sea, or a whale, that thou settest a watch over me? 13 When I say, My bed shall comfort me, my couch shall ease my complaint; 14 Then thou scarest me with dreams, and terrifiest me through visions: 15 So that my soul chooseth strangling, and death rather than my life. 16 I loathe it; I would not live alway: let me alone; for my days are vanity.

7.10.1.en: Therefore I will not refrain my mouth;

7.10.2.en: I will speak in the anguish of my spirit;

7.10.3.en: I will complain in the bitterness of my soul [11].

7.10.4.en: When the prophet David perceived the vanity of temporal life he said: "I was dumb, I opened not my mouth" (Ps 39:9); but Job, knowing the same truth, did not stop speaking, but declared his complaint with bitterness in order to give his last testament to his friends and those around him.

7.10.5.en: It is fitting for us in our last breaths to confess our sins as we praise and thank God, that we may depart in the peace of God instead of complaint and murmuring.

7.10.6.en: * "I also will not refrain my mouth," for the man who is ashamed to confess the evil he has done [refrains his mouth]... Therefore the Psalmist says: [Let us come before his presence with confession] (Ps 95:2). We have received from Solomon: "He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy" (Prov 28:13). It is also written: [The righteous man is the first accuser of himself] (cf. Prov 18:17).

7.10.7.en: * [I will speak in the anguish of my spirit], for "the anguish of the spirit" prepares the tongue for speech, so that there is the voice of confession against the commission of evil. For it is fitting to keep in mind that the corrupt often confess sins, but they boast of them greatly and do not weep over them. But the elect express their bitter condemnation of themselves with tears, which disclose the words of confession. Therefore it is well that, after the blessed Job promised not to restrain his lips, he immediately added the anguish of the spirit.

7.10.8.en: [I will speak in the bitterness of my soul (spirit)]... The bitterness of the spirit has its own tongue in the heart of the righteous, and it speaks more precisely and is listened to more (than the bodily tongue). Therefore he did not say: "I speak in the bitterness of my spirit," but said: [I will speak (converse) with bitterness], since the power of grief takes each sin separately and stirs the mind, numbed, to lamentation.

7.10.10.en: * When you are occupied with some sin, be an accuser of yourself (Prov 18:17), and do not wait for others to bring the accusation. By this you become like a righteous man who accuses himself in the first speech he makes in court, or you are like Job, whom the multitude of the people in the city did not hinder from declaring his crime before all."

7.10.11.en: St. Basil the Great * The Father listens to you while you speak within yourself, and hastens to meet you. When you are still far off He sees you and runs.

7.10.12.en: He looks at what is in your heart, and hastens so that no one may delay you, and even embraces you.

7.10.13.en: His "meeting you" is His foreknowledge, and His "embracing you" is the declaration of His mercy and an expression of His fatherly love.

7.10.14.en: He falls on your neck to raise you, you who have fallen under the weight of sins, and to bring you back to heaven when you have turned toward the earth, that you may seek your Creator.

7.10.15.en: Christ falls on your neck, to deliver your neck from the yoke of bondage, and to make you bear His easy yoke (Mt 11:30)...

7.10.16.en: He falls on your neck by saying: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you" (Mt 11:28-29).

7.10.17.en: Thus the Lord embraces you when you repent.

7.11.0.en: St. Ambrose Am I a sea, or a whale, that thou settest a watch over me? [12]

7.11.1.en: David the Psalmist looked to God as he thought of his passing from the world, so he kept silent with his mouth in order that his heart might praise God and contemplate the glories God has prepared for him; but Job looked at himself and thought of his sufferings, and so was in a raging revolt, and gave himself an excuse by saying: "Am I a sea, or a whale?" [12]. Am I a raging sea without ceasing, that needs to be held to its limits? Or a dragon whose bridle must be held so that it does not devour all the fish of the sea?

7.11.2.en: * I am not in a strength like that of the sea, which You made great among creatures, and for its sake You placed sand around it as a guard, You who by Your command set the sea in its bounds and break its power...

7.11.3.en: Nor have I the malice of the dragon, for You set enmity between him and man.

7.11.4.en: You signified to him to keep himself far from man as his enemy, giving him a warning in this regard: "I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel" (Gen 3:15).

7.11.5.en: In any case: "Thou settest a watch over me" means that You set over me a malicious watcher, the traitor, who observes all my actions and all my words. He examines even my thoughts and betrays me in everything I do.

7.11.6.en: Moreover, he lays to my charge, in the form of an accusation, a matter that was not in my mind. I did not keep Your commandment in order to obtain passing happiness, but I love God for the sake of the life to come, as a faithful servant (Mt 24:25; 25:21, 23). The enemy made him a watcher over me; under his watch he was bound and fettered in a wretched state and with exceedingly cruel trials. And You stretched out the hand of Your help to him, and not to me, therefore the trials came upon me.
